rewrites.summary:
Myanmar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Section 377 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use “shadow laws” — notably Section 30(d) of the Rangoon Police Act, allowing detention of anyone who cannot “satisfactorily account” for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the National Unity Government documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities, with the 2024 Conscription Law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the junta banned seven books for LGBTQ+ content as “obscene.” There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under police-act powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Section 377 criminalises same-sex intimacy — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the police-act "shadow law" is the trans-specific detention mechanism.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: General civil-war risks affect all travelers and are out of scope; the score reflects trans-specific persecution by the junta.

Verdict: avoid entirely.

Media report (January 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; opposition figures recorded LGBT people killed and critically injured since 1 February 2021; a survey of LGBT respondents found most have no confidence in the legal system and most fear repercussions from abusers.

Civil-society submission to an international human-rights process (June 2024): killings of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled areas — a small number dead since the coup; intensified enforcement of a penal-code provision as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

Media report (10 January 2025): the junta banned LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; a historic-era legal provision carries up to 10 years for same-sex conduct; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the February 2021 coup.

Civil-society research (March 2025, based on local research from January 2025): the 2024 conscription law drives queer people into fear and displacement; the penal-code provision carries life imprisonment or a long term, and a historic-era police-act clause on face covering is used specifically against transgender people.

Media report (2 February 2016): a local trans-support organisation — a trans woman describes arrest, stripping, a beating and two weeks' detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work; documents routine police violence against trans women.

Media report (2 November 2018): an outspoken LGBTI advocate with HIV, a restaurant owner, was charged under the penal-code provision over an alleged offence against an employee — the provision in active use, with the community demanding fair media coverage.

Media report (17 October 2015): historic-era criminalisation; arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); local spirit mediums are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.

rewrites.summary:
Cuba is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's most legally transformed countries. The 2019 Constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the 2022 Family Code (66.87% referendum approval) overhauled family law; and trans people can change legal gender — the July 2025 civil-registry reform further eliminated bureaucratic hurdles for name changes. CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme, and Havana has a visible, state-tolerated trans community.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific: Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, the economic crisis has degraded healthcare (hormone availability is unreliable), and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people as trans — the historical UMAP camps era is long past and officially repudiated — but there is also no independent recourse if something goes wrong.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression or documents; low street-hostility in tourist areas; the risk is the general absence of rule-of-law recourse.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The 2022 Family Code overhauled family law (including same-sex marriage) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.localsOnly: The civil-registry LGR reform, CENESEX trans-care programme, and unreliable hormone availability are resident-facing.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Political repression, shortages, and detention powers affect all travelers; LGR mechanics are resident-facing.

blindSourceSummaries: Legal overview (30 May 2026): documents the country's arc from historic forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, cutting cane, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — a 1979 penal-code removal of consensual same-sex acts, the former leader's public acceptance of blame (2010), a 2008 resolution providing trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 constitution (first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 family code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: a labor-code provision bars discrimination on sexual orientation but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, covering orientation, not identity.

Media preview (15 September 2022): the 25 September 2022 family-code referendum — the fourth national vote since 1959 — would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights; opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote against purely to deny the current administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (over one thousand arrestees) and record emigration. Useful context for how contested (rather than nationally enforced) the equality settlement is.

Sympathetic first-person account (23 December 2011) disputing claims of systematic national homophobia — documents the historic camps (conscripts paid a small daily wage), a 1975 declaration-era turning point, and a nationally backed programme run by the sex-education centre: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the top court, and sexual-diversity education. Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.

Media report (21 December 2013): lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate; the sex-education centre proposed extending it to gender identity, disability and HIV status — the trans-specific amendment drew support from some religious and intellectual legislators, and passage of the sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity ban was the confirmed outcome. Predates the 2019 constitution and 2022 family code (superseded in scope, not in error).

Media report (26 May 2018): documents use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — two citizens who filed asylum claims abroad faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned; a woman deported after seeking asylum abroad was detained (19 May 2018); and LGBTI activists remained monitored. Relevant to visitors: the country's hostility toward emigration/asylum, not toward gender expression as such.

rewrites.summary:
Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The buggery law (up to 10 years) is a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners and shapes police culture.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The buggery law is a situational/climate factor; resort vs. non-resort risk differs sharply.

rewrites.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The Grindr ambush robbery pattern is a direct risk for trans visitors using apps.
rewrites.localsOnly: No LGR and no SOGI anti-discrimination protection — resident-facing; the “beaten, stoned and chopped” pattern describes residents.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Decriminalisation status and reform rejections are climate/legal context; no trans-specific statute exists.

blindSourceSummaries: Media report (July 2024): the director of a local transgender coalition says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Media report (November 2024): police warning over cyber criminals — app hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake profiles to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

Media editorial (June 2024): a spate of app-related attacks (almost half a dozen in recent months); a senior police official points to gaps in the law: no specific hate-crime category exists in legislation; the editorial argues the gap must be closed.

Media report (23 August 2024): the ruling party's constitution review committee rejected adding sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution (decision announced at a special convention); an activist said the community has been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection. Documents LGBTQ-rights exclusion from the 2024 constitutional-review process.

Travel/culture profile (August 2012) stating that although homosexuality is illegal, 'the laws are mostly ignored' in practice; describes tourist-facing social scene and local context. Usable as a 2012 non-enforcement baseline; predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling, so dated for current-law purposes.

Media report (21 November 2017): first-person appeal by an activist during his high-court challenge to the country's same-sex criminalisation — he faced up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner; the report carries the litigation campaign. Marks the constitutional challenge that put the criminal law in play.

Media report (23 June 2016): the prime minister told parliament (17 June 2016) the government must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws; cites a local newspaper. Documents the reform-refusal gap in official rhetoric as of 2016.

rewrites.summary:
Ghana is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: “Unnatural carnal knowledge” (up to 3 years) criminalises same-sex conduct — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the lapsed bill would have criminalised identity itself.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 bill never became law (lapsed unassented); its significance is climate/trajectory.

rewrites.summary:
Morocco is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years), and Cairo 52 documents that trans people face de-facto criminalisation under Article 498 morality provisions — arrests based on gender-expression discrepancies and forced outing. The 2026 Cairo 52 report “A Web of Violence” describes a legal-medical-social system of erasure for trans people, including a de facto prohibition on transition care.

Visitor-relevant cases exist: in 2024, Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh, accused by police of being transgender, and alleges she was forced to show her genitals — she spent a month in jail. In 2019, Marrakesh police filmed and humiliated a cross-dressing man after a traffic accident, leaking the video online. There is no LGR framework and police have wide discretion; tourist areas (Marrakesh, Agadir) are more tolerant in practice but the legal exposure is constant.

The Gutierrez case demonstrates that even a cisgender visitor suspected of being trans can face genital inspection and jail.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
rewrites.localsOnly: The de facto transition-care prohibition described in Cairo 52's "A Web of Violence" is resident-facing.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; the 2024 Gutierrez arrest was officially for filming a policeman — the trans-suspicion genital inspection is her allegation, disputed by Morocco.

blindSourceSummaries: Report by a monitoring organisation (January 2026): based on interviews with trans and non-binary people — documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility; the country once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens; one article is weaponised to arrest trans people based on gender expression; no legal gender recognition pathway.

Country review by the same organisation: no specific provisions on transition, but de facto criminalisation under morality provisions (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only; the country's top religious official opposes transition.
Media report (November 2024): a social-media model alleges police forced her to show her genitals over trans suspicions — reported police abuse of a trans woman based on appearance.

Media report (January 2019): police subjected a cross-dresser to online humiliation — after a minor traffic accident, the person was handcuffed and filmed by bystanders and police officers, who also photographed his ID documents and posted them online; he sought asylum abroad. Same-sex conduct is punishable here.

Human-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): one article criminalises 'indecent acts' between persons of the same sex (6 months to 3 years) with wide police discretion and arbitrary arrests; many people were charged with same-sex relations in 2018; a human-rights organisation documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; no legal gender recognition; public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment; authorities block LGBTIQ organisations.

Human-rights organisation report (April 2018) on LGBT activism in the region: includes the country's criminalisation provision — an article used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression — and an annex of similar laws across the region.
LGBTI organisation world survey (May 2008): world survey of laws prohibiting same-sex activity between consenting adults — country-by-country legal survey including this country.

Media report (September 2014): an international human-rights body adopted the sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity resolution — international context for human-rights scrutiny of countries including this one.
